ARCHAEOLOGICAL SCIENCE 249
Human remains and evidence
BOX 5.6
of warfare: Towton Moor
Archaeology rarely provides indisputable evidence of
the consequences of warfare because sites of battles
rarely survive undisturbed, and damage visible on
human bones may be the result of individual injuries
or acts of violence, rather than actual warfare. One
exceptional case is the mass grave at Towton Moor
in North Yorkshire, found on the site of a known
battle that took place during the Wars of the Roses
in AD 1461. The excavation uncovered a shallow grave
containing around thirty-seven individuals, interred
with little sign of respect or normal burial practices
(Fiorato et al. 2007: 186). Palaeopathology provided
detailed information, including evidence for the
multiple wounds suffered by many of the individuals
in previous conficts. The examination was able to
explore the patterns of wounds associated with

DNA and disease: the archaeology
BOX 5.7
of tuberculosis
Diseases in past populations have traditionally been identifed
when they left visible traces on bones. Tuberculosis (TB) is one
such disease, spread through sneezing and coughing, or by
infected meat and milk. If untreated, it can spread to the bone
and the lymphatic system, leading to changes which can be
detected in bones. This image, from Bedhampton in Hampshire,
is an early medieval example of such changes. In this individual,
TB has led to the destruction of the vertebrae, leading to collapse,
and would have given a ‘hunchback’ appearance to the person
in life. This technique cannot, however, recognise the presence
of the illnesses in people where it left no evidence on the actual
skeleton – around 95% of all cases. This means that for some
time understanding of the development and movement of TB
relied on those instances recognised through palaeopathology.
Studies using ancient DNA, however, have signifcantly enhanced
this picture by looking for evidence of the presence of the TB
bacterium in human skeletons. This has provided a clearer picture (Image source: Charlotte Roberts,
of how and where TB developed and how it has spread through Durham University).
human populations, from its origins in 9000 years BP to the
present day (Spigelman et al. 2015). This research has wider implications for modern health, as TB is
still one of the most deadly diseases, particularly in developing nations.

Movement and migration:
BOX 5.8
Bronze Age Beaker burials
The early Bronze Age in Britain is characterised by
burials associated with distinctive pottery beakers (like
the one shown here); similar burials have been found
all around the Atlantic fringe of north-western Europe.
There has been a long debate amongst archaeologists
about whether the individuals buried with beakers were
migrants from elsewhere in Europe or locals who had
adopted new burial rites (a helpful summary can be found
in Crellin 2020: 187–95). Analysis of both strontium and
oxygen isotopes and aDNA has been employed in an
attempt to answer this question, and it has shown that
not only was there a large-scale western movement of
the population across Europe (Olalde et al. 2018) but that
the early Bronze Age in Britain was indeed characterised
by incoming migrating populations (Needham 2007;
Parker Pearson et al. 2019). The exceptionally rich burial
of the so-called Amesbury Archer provides one of the
most high-profle examples of this. Despite being buried
(Image source: Ashmolean Museum of Art
in Wiltshire, southern Britain, oxygen isotope analysis
and Archaeology/Heritage Images).
from his tooth enamel indicated that as a child he lived
in the Alps region, in either Switzerland, Austria or Germany (Chenery and Evans 2011). However,
through the recent ‘Beaker People Project’ Parker-Pearson et al. (2019) have undertaken extensive
isotopic analyses of Britain’s Bronze Age populations in conjunction with a review of the archaeological
evidence, and they have argued for a more nuanced reading of the picture in the UK. Their work has
demonstrated that whilst there was indeed migration into Britain, this is likely to have been from
small groups over generations, rather than any concerted ‘wave’ of migrants. Furthermore, they
have shown that the Bronze Age in Britain was characterised by signifcant internal mobility (Parker-
Pearson et al. 2019: 447–49) and regionally distinct material culture practices. This complex set of
results demonstrates that V. Gordon Childe’s hypothesis that these people represented a single
migration of itinerant metalworkers from Europe (see Chapter 6) was a gross oversimplifcation.
Instead, there is now a substantial body of work which demonstrates that ‘becoming Bronze Age’
was not a single, linear, unifed process but rather something which was regionally variable, ‘messy,
complex, and multiple’ (Crellin 2020: 224).

ARCHAEOLOGICAL SCIENCE 255
Isola Sacra: diet and migration in Ancient Rome
BOX 5.9
In the frst to third centuries AD, the city of Rome had a population of around one million people and
was the centre of an extensive empire. Historical evidence suggests there was signifcant migration
into the city from all over the Roman Empire (Garnsey 1987). What can archaeological science tell
us about the origin of these people and their diet? Analysis of the cemetery of Isola Sacra, close
to Ostia (the port of Rome at the mouth of the river Tiber), has indicated the origin of the people
buried there. Analysis of teeth revealed that a signifcant proportion of the population had migrated
to the city as children, with oxygen isotope evidence suggesting that a large number came from
the regions to the north and east of Rome, while one individual probably originated in North Africa.
Analysis of the diet using isotopic analysis of the cemetery population suggested that these people
had consumed a mixture of seafood and food derived from land. There were, however, signifcant
differences; evidence showed that older individuals had consumed high-status foods (such as fsh
and olive oil), while children had a poorer diet based on plants (Prowse et al. 2004, 2005, 2007).
Whilst some scholars have subsequently highlighted that the isotopic data from Isola Sacra is quite
different from the epigraphic data (that is the inscriptions on the tombs) (Bruun 2010), Prowse (2016)
has made the important point that only a very small portion of the population could afford such
inscriptions (mostly elite men). Thus, the isotopic data plays an important role in enabling us to learn
about ‘people who couldn’t necessarily afford an inscription, which is the vast majority of the Roman
population’ (Prowse 2016: 217). The image below shows some of the second century AD ‘house-
tombs’ from Isola Sacra.
(Image source: Robert Witcher, Durham University).

Figure 5.10 Human bioarchaeology is an area with enormous potential for research. Much work has been
done already to trace people’s origins through traces of lead in their teeth or to establish the role of fsh and
other marine foods in people’s diets. DNA studies offer further insights, including our understanding of the
colonisation of the globe by humans. This map shows the process of human dispersal derived from both
fossil remains and analysis of mtDNA; the latter, based on the different haplogroups, indicates that greatest
genetic diversity is found in Africa, implying that humans have lived there longest. Genetic similarities can
also demonstrate the origins of human ancestors: for example, America was colonised from Siberia, and New
Zealand more recently from Polynesia. Allied to fossil and other archaeological evidence, a detailed map of the
chronology and process of human dispersal across the globe can be recognised.

Figure 5.15 An example highlighting the value of XRF for source analysis can be found in the case of an
obsidian artefact held in the British Museum known as ‘John Dee’s Mirror’, pictured here. Dee was a Tudor
magus and occultist, as well as scientifc advisor and astrologer to Queen Elizabeth I. Dee was fascinated with
using mirrors and other objects to contact spirits and angels (Campbell et al. 2021). Part of his collection for this
purpose was a polished obsidian mirror which, after his death, passed through various hands and ended up in
the British Museum. There has been some debate about the source of the mirror, with some suggesting that it
matched typologically similar Aztec pieces, whilst others suggested that it was a European forgery. To resolve
this question pXRF analysis was undertaken on Dee’s mirror, as well as on a series of geological samples from
known Mexican obsidian sources. These comparative analyses confrmed that the mirror derived from the
Pachuca obsidian source, which was heavily used by the Aztecs (Campbell et al. 2021).

Roman coins
BOX 5.10
The use of information derived from the analysis of metals is not restricted to the prehistoric period.
Roman metallurgy has been extensively studied through examination of ores, ingots, coins and
manufactured objects. Evidently alloys could be prepared very accurately to match the properties of
the metal to the function of the end product (Greene 1986: 143–49). Of particular interest is the way
that the principal Roman silver coin, the denarius (pictured below), gradually lost its content of silver
as successive emperors debased the metal in a desperate attempt to outstrip infation (Archibald and
Cowell 1993; Cope et al. 1997). Under Augustus (27 BC–AD 14) denarii were as pure as possible, and
contained 95% silver, but by the middle of the third century AD, when infation and political chaos reigned,
the silver content had fallen to between 1 and 3% (Walker 1976–8). Coins left the mint with a thin silver
coating that soon wore off in use, leaving a coin that could only with diffculty be differentiated from
contemporary bronze issues (King and Hedges 1974). The difference between early and late examples is
obvious to the eye, but analysis has charted the decline in detail; it provides an interesting commentary
on the contemporary economy and the political problems of rulers who authorised debasements
(Greene 1986: 60–62). ED-XRF analysis (see p. 264) is used to analyse coins in this way, determining
the debasement of coinage at certain periods (Engelhardt 2006).
Pictured here is a hoard, likely deposited in the late second century AD, consisting of 101 Roman
silver denarii. This hoard was reported through the UK’s Portable Antiquities Scheme, who identifed
that ‘the earliest coin in the group is a legionary denarius of Mark Antony (issued c. 32BC–31BC) and
the latest a denarius of Commodus dated to AD 190–191’.
(Image source: National Museums Liverpool, CC BY-SA 2.0 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/
by-sa/2.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

Figure 5.19 The tenth-century AD Viking boat burial from the Ardnamurchan Peninsula (Harris et al. 2017)
provides a good example of the important work of conservators. Most of the artefacts within this burial
were very corroded when they were found, as the top left image (a) of the sword, in situ, demonstrates.
However, conservation work stabilised the artefacts, preventing further deterioration and, in the case of the
sword, an X-ray (b) enabled further investigation and demonstrated the multiple materials it was made of.
Conservator Pieta Greaves was then able to undertake careful cleaning of the pommel and guard to reveal
beautiful decoration made of silver and copper wire (c, d).

• Placing interpretation and ‘theory’ into a standalone chapter does not mean that we consider
them separate from ‘practice’, any more than our other chapters imply clear dividing lines be-
tween science and dating, or excavation and feldwork.
• This chapter presents a concise overview of developments in archaeological theory since the
early twentieth century. These developments coincided with some fundamental changes in out-
look that accompanied the end of the Second World War and the beginning of the Cold War. An
optimistic and confdent approach called the New Archaeology emerged by the 1960s, charac-
terised by processualism, which attempted to make the subject more ‘scientifc’.
• From the 1980s postprocessual archaeology developed. This is very important because much
writing about archaeology – and about prehistory in particular – has been caught up in wider
intellectual movements associated with modernism and postmodernism. Structuralism and
poststructuralism have had profound effects upon culture in general, from art and literature to
the sciences, and archaeology refects this wider situation.
• Philosophies that have looked critically at modernism have brought positive benefts to inter-
pretive archaeology, which pays greater attention to individual experiences than to abstract
processes. These philosophies have raised the profle of issues such as gender, race, ethnicity,
sexuality and disability and pioneered approaches to material culture and the body, including
materiality and fragmentation.
• The most recent theoretical developments in archaeology take interpretive archaeology a step
further, arguing that a focus solely on humans as separate from and superior to the material
world limits what we can say about the present and the past. We will explore this ‘ontological
turn’ towards non-human-centred posthuman, new materialist archaeologies.

This is the facade of a ‘megalithic’ chambered tomb (Cairnholy I, Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland).
These elaborate stone monuments are found in many parts of western Europe, Scandinavia and
Germany and attracted much attention from early antiquaries. They usually contain stone-lined
chambers, often with long entrance passageways. Some are architecturally sophisticated, with
enormous stones or elaborate vaulting, and may bear geometric or curvilinear carving. Where the
contents of the chambers survive, excavation usually reveals collective burials of large numbers of
individuals, or parts of individuals.
Monumental stone architecture appeared in Egypt soon after 3000 BC and reached remarkable
sophistication in monuments such as Zoser’s step pyramid at Saqqara, c. 2650 BC. Tombs with stone
passageways and vaulted chambers existed in the Aegean area around 1600 BC, and archaeologists
adopting a ‘diffusionist’ interpretation assumed that these provided the inspiration for chambered
tombs further north and west. In the 1960s, radiocarbon dating began to produce dates around 3000
BC for megalithic tombs – too early for the supposed prototypes in the Aegean and even earlier than
the frst stone architecture in Egypt; calibration according to the tree-ring curve and new dates from
Brittany actually placed several before 4000 BC. ‘Quite obviously, if they have their ultimate origin in
the Aegean, this must have been a long time before 3000 BC. Yet there are no collective built tombs

MAKING SENSE OF THE PAST 287
in the Aegean until after this date. The Breton dates, even without calibration, make nonsense of the
diffusionist case’ (Renfrew 1973a: 89–90).
Megalithic tombs, circles and alignments underwent intense mathematical analysis from the
1960s onwards to explore their astronomical signifcance (Ruggles 1999); this form of study coincided
with the expansion of space science and computers. The scientifc outlook of New Archaeology
attempted to explain the megaliths in terms of identical patterns of social behaviour taking place
independently in many parts of Europe. Postprocessual interpretations have explored how
megaliths and other monuments shape, refect and reinforce concepts of time, memory, ancestry
and identity amongst communities and individuals. At the height of club-culture involving hypnotic
dance music and drugs in the 1990s it was suggested that the acoustic properties of megaliths
would enhance sound and cause physical sensations in people involved in ceremonies (Watson and
Keating 1999). Recent advances in radiocarbon dating are leading to further transformation, refning
the chronologies of these monuments even further (Chapter 4; Bayliss et al. 2007). Revised dating
of Neolithic chambered tombs in central-southern England, through the application of Bayesian
statistics to radiocarbon dates, indicates that depositions of the remains of dead people took place in
them for relatively short periods of time – decades rather than centuries (Bayliss et al. 2007; Bayliss
et al. 2007). Postprocessual theories refect the concepts of agency and individualism, which have
dominated much of archaeological theory since the 1980s, rather than the traditional explanation of
commemorating ancestors (Parker-Pearson and Ramilisonina 1998a; Edmonds 1999). More recent
non-anthropocentric (that is, non-human-centred) approaches have explored how such monuments
represent messy assemblages of people, places and things which together have different effects
through time (Fowler 2013; Harris 2021b). Studies of such monuments are also looking at their
reception and understanding by later communities, including our own (Chippindale 2004; Darvill
2006; Darvill et al. 2019).
Changing interpretations of megaliths underline the diffculty of making sense of the past. This
probably helps to explain the attraction of alternative explanations linked to lost civilisations, extra-
terrestrial contacts or utopian New Age visions of the past (something we return to in Box 7.1).

Nationalism and archaeology
BOX 6.2
Archaeology has been used in diverse ways to
emphasise different aspects of people’s pasts,
while the changing popularity of different periods
or research themes has frequently refected
contemporary political preoccupations. Although
the use of archaeology by nationalists is well
known in the context of Nazi Germany, there
have been many other examples. In France,
Napoleon III conducted excavations at Alésia in
the late nineteenth century in order to investigate
the site of the last stand by Vercingetorix against
the Roman conquerors in 52 BC (described by the
victorious Julius Caesar in his autobiographical
Gallic Wars). The growth of national identity in
nineteenth-century France naturally focused
on the leader of the Gallic resistance and led
to extensive research into the Late Iron Age
culture conquered by the Romans. A statue
of Vercingetorix (pictured here) was raised by
Napoleon III at Alésia in 1865, with a plaque bearing
a quotation from Caesar: ‘United Gaul, forming a
single nation, animated by a common spirit, can
defy the universe’. Since Napoleon III, Alésia and
other sites like Bibracte, as well as Vercingetorix
himself, have been used by a variety of French

Britain leaving Europe (Bonacchi 2022). Nationalism can be more complex than it frst appears, however;

increasingly being constructed through online sources, and especially social media, as part of the rise in
populist nationalism in the frst part of the twenty-frst century (Bonacchi 2022).

Reconstructing past societies: hierarchies,
BOX 6.3
heterarchies and social complexity
One of the most challenging and contentious aspects of studying the past is reconstructing and
understanding how past societies worked. If we consider how many anthropologists, sociologists
and philosophers attempt to understand the complexities of modern-day societies, the challenge
of reconstructing a past society from its material remains alone can be appreciated. As discussion
of archaeological thought makes clear, how archaeologists view past societies has been infuenced
not just by the ways in which they collected archaeological evidence but also by their personal
political viewpoints (for example, Marxism or Darwinism) and the contemporary societies they
inhabit, from autocracies to democracies. One of the most signifcant questions, particularly about
prehistoric societies, has been whether they were hierarchical, with defned social classes and
elites controlling other groups, or heterarchical, more equally based societies where power was
less stratifed or where power might shift between individuals and communities of more equal
status (Crumley 2015).
For much of archaeology’s development, antiquarians and archaeologists came from societies
that were highly ranked (either by aristocracies or the class divisions of early industrialised societies).
Archaeologists themselves were also usually from the upper classes of such societies. Combined
with contemporary thinking that suggested a hierarchical society was the normal order of human
organisation, this led them to envision past societies in a generally hierarchical way and to study and
defne the elites in past societies (see Box 3.4 in Crumley 2001: 19). This led, amongst other things,
to many analyses of cemeteries which used grave goods in burials to rank individuals in the past
societies, for example the rich burials of Early Iron Age central Europe (Frankenstein and Rowlands
1978). This appeared to provide well defned social systems where one could even identify the status
of an individual from the size of their tumulus and the nature of the grave goods buried with them. Such
studies also usually assumed that men and warriors were naturally at the top of any social system.
In the 1960s American anthropologists, such as Marshal Sahlins and Morton Fried, in an attempt
to classify societies, ranked them into different forms of increasing social complexity (below).

MAKING SENSE OF THE PAST 297
Whilst the models differed somewhat, they emphasised the idea that societies could be placed into
broader categories and that these communities evolved into ever more complex social systems. This
continued to suggest that human societies developed through stages of social evolution (see p.
287–90) and could readily be related to stages of human societies. For some, most of later prehistory
must therefore have been dominated by some form of chiefdom societies (Renfrew 1973b; Haas
2001; Barker 2009).

The New Archaeologists of the 1960s and 1970s tended to classify prehistoric societies in these
terms, suggesting that the size and complexity of many monuments, such as Neolithic henge
monuments like Stonehenge (Renfrew 1973b), the hillforts of the European Iron Age (Cunliffe 1984)
or the centralised pueblos of New Mexico (Creamer 2001), must have been constructed through
the control of established elites. Such approaches also believed that the territories of chiefdoms

298 MAKING SENSE OF THE PAST
many that the entire concept of chiefdoms as unified social systems suitable for describing
communities in Mississippian North America or prehistoric Europe is overly simplistic (e.g.
Pauketat 2007; Hill 2006; cf. Haas 2001; Thurston and Fernández-Götz 2022). They suggest that
ranking societies on the basis of grave goods is to place Western values on objects, and to make
assumptions about the role of elements such as swords as markers of social status, ignoring the
fact that such items may have very different roles in other societies (e.g. Bradley 1998). Study of
the Mississippian mounds (Box 1.3) has long been argued as evidence of chiefdom communities
where power resided in the hands of elites, but from the work of anthropologists it is clear that
even large monuments and complex social systems can be constructed by communities where no
established elite exists (Pauketat 2007).
Chris Tilley (1984) and others, from a neo-Marxist viewpoint, have also suggested that in many
societies there is not always a clear correlation between expressions of power and wealth and
the real nature of a society. Elsewhere, highly ranked societies may not express status and power
through differences in burial or even in size of houses or settlement but through elements which
are more diffcult to detect archaeologically, such as the number of cattle they own. Through the
ethnographic study of non-Western societies, and a more sophisticated appreciation of how our
own societies work, archaeologists have increasingly reconsidered the variation and complexity of
social systems; to defne societies as hierarchical or heterarchical is to oversimplify and generalise
the complex systems of many societies, even hunter-gatherer communities. The debate as to how
to reconstruct societies continues in many areas of archaeology and represents perhaps one of the
most contentious questions for the discipline.

craft production may broaden our understanding of such activities in pre-industrial societies. Ethnoarchaeology,

Figure 6.6 Can hominin and early human behaviour and communication be deduced from artefacts? The
evolution of cognitive abilities – notably the development of language – is only indirectly refected by this kind
of evidence. Stone artefacts reveal changing conceptual approaches to tool making. Some of the earliest
‘Oldowan’ examples from sites in East Africa are pebbles with fakes knocked off to create a sharper end (A),
perhaps for hacking through animal hide and tough fesh; the fakes could be used for cutting. Acheulian bifaces
(B) were made by removing a very large fake from a prepared core and applying pressure to remove further
fakes and produce a sharp cutting edge along both sides and at the point. Such ‘hand-axes’ are found not only
in Africa but in other areas of the world colonised by Homo erectus. Neanderthals and other early humans
extended the range of tools by striking and retouching fakes of various shapes and sizes (C, D). Anatomically
modern humans seem to have been the frst to strike long thin fakes from large cores and to adapt these
‘blades’ (or parts of them) into a wider range of specialised tools by further faking (E). Some artefacts were
extraordinarily thin and carefully faked, to the extent that their production may have been partly for ‘show’ (F).
Do the variety, virtuosity and rapid typological change seen in artefacts associated with ‘anatomically modern
humans’ indicate higher cognitive and manipulative skills than were possessed by Neanderthals, or do they
refect adaptation to rapid climatic change after a long period of stability?.

Phenomenology: postprocessualism and
BOX 6.4
landscape archaeology
Phenomenological approaches have been
particularly infuential in landscape archaeology.
Tilley’s study of Neolithic monuments in
southern England (1994) examined Neolithic
perceptions of the world, focusing on what
could be seen from certain locations and how
movement through the landscape may have
affected perceptions. These studies have been
inspired by the work of anthropologists such
as Keith Basso (1996) who examined how non-
Western societies in North America conceive
and perceive the landscapes around them.
Tilley used refexive concepts to place the
feelings and perceptions of modern viewers
at the heart of his study. Such models have
been followed up by others who have focused
on how monuments might have been created
in reference to the landscape around them
(Cummings et al. 2002; Cummings and Whittle
2003). Using such perspectives one might
question, for example, what the signifcance
is of the location of the prehistoric rock art
(shown in the photo) below this prominent hill
(Image source: Tom Moore).
in Northumberland with commanding views
of the surrounding landscape. These approaches are by no means universally accepted, however,
and have been criticised by some for failing to take into account the multiplicity of embodied
experiences in the past (Brück 2005). Other practitioners of landscape archaeology have argued that
phenomenological studies neglect practical details (Fleming 2008), as well as for broader failures:
‘The current preoccupation with how prehistoric people perceived past landscapes . . . leave it
wilfully unclear whether the perceptions proposed are those of the investigator or the past people
being studied’ (Shennan 2004: 3).

wrote while hiding from the Nazis in a house (now a museum) in Amsterdam. Her lively diaries have helped
subsequent generations of young readers to empathise with her persecution, betrayal and untimely death.
A touring exhibition from the Anne Frank Museum keeps her memory alive and supports campaigns against
racism; when it visited York in 1998 the city was reminded about an episode of persecution that happened
there in AD 1190. York’s Jews were attacked by a mob and sought refuge in a wooden tower on this mound.
They committed mass suicide as an alternative to being baptised or killed; the wooden tower was destroyed
by fre and replaced in stone. This powerful image demonstrates the potential for linking sites from the past to

Figure 6.10 The search continues for new fossils
to help increase our understanding of intermediate
species between apes and humans. Much of the
skeleton of an australopithecine around three million
years old (commonly known as Lucy) was found
at Afar in Ethiopia in 1974, followed in 1978 by the
discovery of fossil footprints of a similar age at Laetoli
in Tanzania (Turnbaugh et al. 2002: 231–32). This life-
sized model was created for an exhibition about human
evolution in the Yorkshire Museum in 2001 to illustrate
these small ape-like hominins who walked upright.
However, knowledge about their behaviour is complete
guesswork and is largely based on observations of
modern primates such as chimpanzees. This model
may make them appear more ‘human’ than ‘ape’
by suggesting a family group consisting of a strong
man protecting a woman and child. Does it also
have (perhaps unconsciously) a rather conservative
ideological role, suggesting that the two-parent family
unit – with a dominant male – is an ancient and ‘natural’
way of life? Alison Jolly has commented on a similar
model: ‘Lucy is judged female just because she/he was
petite. . . . If australopithecines lived in fssion–fusion,
male-bonded groups like chimps, the females may well
have mated promiscuously. . . . Only later, long after the
evolution of both concealed ovulation and bipedality,
would more monogamous bonds lead to private sex
and a father’s paternal obligations to his own beloved
young’ (Jolly 1999: 357, 364–65). Jolly’s comments are
echoed in Dowson’s analysis of similar representations
of heterosexual families through time at Leicester’s
Jewry Wall Museum (Dowson 2006). There is a clear
message: every picture of the past is an artefact of
the present and will embody modern concepts (Moser
1998); awareness of gender, sexuality, race, ethnicity

7
CHAPTER 7
The past in the present
and the future
• The fnal chapter in this volume begins by considering where archaeology is in the early twenty-
frst century.
• Drawing upon everything we saw in Chapter 6 around the changing intellectual climate of ar-
chaeological theory and contemporary social concerns, it considers how we make sense of the
past in the present, examining archaeology and the public, as well as heritage management.
• This chapter then considers the future, exploring how archaeology has played a role in under-
standings of the current epoch, the Anthropocene, and how studies of the past may inform
responses to the global climate crisis.
• This section also examines how archaeologists can play a role in protecting archaeology and
heritage for future generations. But what do we mean by ‘the future’, and for whom, and for
what kind of futures, are we preserving the past?
• Finally, it concludes by considering what it is to be an archaeologist today and what this might
mean for the most important element of future archaeology: you, the reader.

344 THE PAST IN THE PRESENT AND THE FUTURE
Are all visions of the past equal?
BOX 7.1
Pseudo-archaeology
One of the greatest challenges
of refexive and postmodern
approaches to archaeology
is multivocality. If we
acknowledge that more than
one view or narrative account
of the past is valid, and we are
open to refection about our own
views, we should recognise
that our models of the past are
heavily infuenced by Western
cultural expectations. This
problem can be addressed in
archaeological research in a
number of interesting ways, for
example by incorporating the (Image source: Getty Stock Images).
views of different people into
investigations (as discussed in
chapter 6). However, when faced with ‘pseudo-archaeology’, the problems become more diffcult.
Alternative archaeological stories by writers such as Erich von Däniken and Graham Hancock have
gained a large following and enduring popularity. They tend to explain ‘mysterious’ archaeological
sites (such as the Egyptian pyramids shown here) and artefacts in terms of extra-terrestrial infuences
or lost civilisations which professional archaeologists deliberately ignore (Feder 2005; G Fagan
2006). Conventional archaeologists examine data and seek to interpret them, and then revise their
interpretations in the light of new evidence. Pseudo-archaeologists create an overarching theory frst,
which they then seek to prove by amassing evidence to support it – frequently overlooking intricacies
and inconsistencies and ignoring conventional archaeological research (G Fagan 2006: 27–30). Such
stories are not necessarily harmless fun;
All too often the claim ‘Aliens built X’ is built upon the assumption that ‘Non-white indige-
nous people Y could not possibly have built X’, while many ‘lost civilisation’ narratives posit
white-skinned settlers who pre-date and/or were wiped out by the apparently indigenous
populations in countries such as New Zealand and the United States. These narratives provide
the blueprints or more commonly post hoc justifcations for colonialism and genocide. Even
apparently ‘harmless’ alternative archaeologies such as the Pagan campaigners for the reburial
of archaeological human remains in the UK can encode strongly nationalist and white-suprem-
acist assumptions within their mythologies.
(Moshenska 2017c: 136)
Furthermore, pseudo-archaeology can also have negative impacts on the presentation of genuine
archaeological sites. In the Balkans, for example, attempts to ‘prove’ the existence of enormous
stone pyramids (which archaeologists regard as natural geological formations) may have had a
detrimental impact on the preservation of Bosnia’s real archaeological heritage (Harding 2007;
Moshenska 2017c).

THE PAST IN THE PRESENT AND THE FUTURE 345
Pseudo-archaeology is not necessarily deliberately dishonest. However, for some the desire to
ensure that their version of the past is accepted has been so strong that they have manufactured
archaeological evidence to ‘prove’ their beliefs. The most famous British example was the faking of
a human ancestor at Piltdown in the nineteenth century (Russell 2003); it was only revealed as a
fraudulent combination of a much later human skull and modern orangutan bones in the 1950s. More
recently an archaeologist in Japan was found to have repeatedly faked the discovery of Palaeolithic
artefacts (G. Fagan 2006: xiii). Fagan (2006: 367) recommends that the best option for archaeologists
is to ‘ask hard questions, probe and expose. Critique after all is the heart of true scholarship’; we would
add that archaeologists should also produce alternative explanations based on a thorough critical
evaluation of the evidence. The separate teams of archaeologists who argue for an interpretation of
Stonehenge either as a healing centre or as a monument commemorating the dead have both tested
their views by feldwork and excavation, and they would undoubtedly abandon their current views if
confronted by evidence which did not support them.

Roman fort that was completely invisible in 1970 in a location dominated by ship building became the centre
of a new leisure attraction in 2001 – by which time most of the local shipyards had closed. Lottery funding
was absolutely essential to this attempt to generate tourism in an otherwise unpromising urban environment
adapting to a post-industrial age.

Heritage management: state protection
BOX 7.2
Deciding which archaeological sites should receive legal protection is not as straightforward as it
might sound. Historic England’s criteria for scheduling an archaeological site are subdivided into
eighteen different guides for the different types of site that might be scheduled. Each of these
guides helps provide further detail around a list of specifc things that DCMS has specifed should be
considered for the selection of Scheduled Monuments. These include:
• The archaeological or historical interest of the site
• Extent of survival
• Rarity
• Representivity, either through diversity or because of one important attribute
• Importance of the period to which the monument dates
• Fragility or vulnerability of the site
• Connection to other monuments, or group value
• Potential to contribute to our information, understanding and appreciation
• Extent of documentation enhancing the monument’s signifcance
(DCMS 2013)
Many of the categories are highly subjective. For example, ‘importance of the period’ may well
change as research interests shift and new fnds provoke reanalysis of individual periods (see Box
3.5). The question of ‘value’ in archaeological remains is likely to be culturally specifc and to refect
changing archaeological and political priorities (Darvill 2005; Smith 2006; Jones 2017; and see
Section 7.2.3). The NHPA in the US has similar criteria for the signifcance of a monument, although
the emphasis is on the association of a monument with historical events or people. This may refect a
categorisation that prioritises historical rather than prehistoric monuments, although it also includes
a broad category ‘having yielded, or likely to yield, information important in prehistory or history’ – a
far broader defnition than that used by Historic England to schedule monuments (Neumann and
Sanford 2001: 33) – although something of this broadness is captured in the notion of ‘heritage
assets’ introduced in England’s National Planning Policy Framework.

Tourism and heritage: Kenilworth Castle
BOX 7.3
Heritage management is often
as much a matter of encouraging
tourism and visitor numbers as
the preservation of archaeological
monuments. At Kenilworth Castle
in Warwickshire, English Heritage
spent £3 million in the frst decade
of the 2000s on aspects of the site
related to Queen Elizabeth I and
her ‘favourite’, Robert Dudley, Earl
of Leicester. Part of this money
was spent on conservation and
new exhibitions in the castle’s
Tudor gatehouse. More than £2
(Image source: Nilfanion, CC BY-SA 4.0 https://creativecommons.
million was spent on a controversial
org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/, via Wikimedia Commons)
attempt to recreate the elaborate
terrace and garden described in Robert Langham’s contemporary account of Elizabeth’s visit in 1575
(Furnivall 1907: 48–53; Keay and Watkins 2013). This project was a matter of simulation, rather than
reconstruction, since no trace of the original layout was recovered by excavation to verify Langham’s
account, apart from the position of a fountain and some chips of the Italian marble from which the
fountain was made.
Some people question whether national heritage bodies should spend a large amount of money
(much of it from taxpayers) on this kind of simulation instead of concentrating on conserving and
conducting research into the surviving structures. Should gardens remain the speciality of charitable
organisations (such as the National Trust) and privately fnanced country houses that rely heavily on
them for attracting much-needed income from visitors? Or should state-funded heritage bodies also
compete for visitors in this way?
English Heritage’s publicity declared that the Elizabethan Garden was, ‘once again, ft for a Queen’.
In contrast, a reviewer on a garden history website regretted that the wooden features did not match
the quality of Tudor craftsmanship: ‘This project looks as though it belongs in an upscale garden
centre near the M25’ (Turner 2009). The judgements of visitors will vary, as will the opinions of
historians about the reliability of Langham’s description of the temporary garden and its structures
and ornaments constructed in 1575. There is, however, no doubt that the new wooden aviary, obelisks
and fences, the marble fountain and the elaborate fowerbeds will require expensive maintenance
for the foreseeable future (Dix 2014). Will the costs be recovered by increased numbers of visitors to
Kenilworth Castle, or will less glamorous conservation and preservation projects elsewhere suffer?

THE PAST IN THE PRESENT AND THE FUTURE 359
Community co-production of heritage:
BOX 7.4
the ‘ACCORD project’
The ACCORD (Archaeology Community Co-Production of Research Data) Project was made up of
heritage professionals from the education and outreach charity Archaeology Scotland and the then Royal
Commission for Ancient and Historical Monuments Scotland (now part of Historic Environment Scotland),
along with academics from the University of Manchester and the Glasgow School of Art (Maxwell 2017).
They worked with ten different community heritage groups across Scotland ‘to create 3D records and
models of heritage places of signifcance to them’ (Jones et al. 2018: 337 – original emphasis). The project
used co-design and co-production methodologies which aimed to shift relationships from the traditional
model that gives power to experts and instead create a more symmetrical relationship between all involved.
‘The interests, agendas and values of the groups concerned, informed the heritage places we recorded
and modelled, creating visualisations of “places of signifcance” as defned by the groups themselves’
(Jones et al. 2018: 342). These ranged from prehistoric monuments and historic buildings to memorials,
sculptures, rock art and even graffti. In each case the value of the heritage site to the local community was
very different to offcial heritage values (Box 7.2), with sites valued for their contribution to distinctive local
or regional identities and to sub-cultures that have rarely been associated with heritage, such as climbing.
The processes of community co-creation of heritage resources fostered the strengthening of community
relationships and also stimulated new discourses about heritage value which went on to shape heritage
policy and be included in the formal National Monument Record for Scotland.
The images here show the ‘ACCORD Project’s’ work in progress with the Dumbarton Rock (‘Dumby’)
climbers. Dumbarton Rock has a long history which fts with more authorised accounts of heritage,
represented by the presence of Dumbarton Castle. However, the Dumby climbers’ work countered this
traditional view of heritage at the site as they chose to chart the heritage of climbing and associated graffti on
the rock (Hale et al. 2017). The group used photogrammetry to create three-dimensional representations of
the graffti. The images pictured show, clockwise from top left, (a) taking photographs of one of the boulders
for photogrammetry; (b) co-design in action; (c) a photogrammetric model of Pongo boulder; (d) processing
images in the feld (Jones et al. 2018: 346).

Figure 7.5 ‘It’s police vs travellers again. Welcome to the English summer’ declared the cover of the Guardian
media magazine The Editor, 25 June 1999. This image was taken at the same time. Stonehenge is England’s
most famous archaeological site, despite the impossibility of knowing its original purpose and the diffculty of
explaining traces of construction phases that accumulated over several thousand years. The summer solstice
has attracted Druids in fowing robes since the nineteenth century, along with a large number of New Age
travellers and hippies from the 1970s. The response has varied from near-total exclusion in the 1990s to a
more open policy from 2000. In June 1999 fencing was torn down and the monument invaded after the
police’s four-mile exclusion zone was declared illegal in the High Court. Stonehenge epitomises the problems
of heritage management in the face of conficting demands. Does the State have the right (and duty) to protect
it – with riot police if necessary? Should the desire of modern pagans to celebrate the midsummer sunrise be
prioritised – even if it means putting the structure at risk?.
(Image source: Adrian Sherratt/Alamy Stock Photo).

Figure 7.6 Richardson and Pickering (2021) have used the format of a comic to explore the complexities of how
Stonehenge is interpreted and understood by archaeologists and by non-heritage specialists. We reproduce
pages 5 and 6 here, which express the variety of ‘what people think it is’. The authors argue that laying the
interpretations out in comic format provides an important way to understand the contemporary relevance of
Stonehenge. In turn, ‘understanding what the wider public might understand about archaeology means we
can support more responsive public engagement, improve access & storytelling, & have a better view of the
role that archaeology plays in informing our national & individual identities’ (Richardson and Pickering 2021: 8).

Figure 7.7 This is a reconstruction of a street from the Middle Ages at Archeon, a theme park close to Amsterdam
in the Netherlands. The park contains reconstructions of buildings from prehistory to the Middle Ages excavated
in various parts of the Netherlands and displays involve actors in period dress. In contrast to pseudo-archaeology
(Box 7.1), it focuses on the ordinary rather than the exotic: ‘In Archeon you can meet the living past of the

a building than a foundation, part of a wall painting or a discoloration of the soil. So, what did such a building
look like? Who lived there? What sort of things did those people do? In Archeon you can step right into such a
building. Meet the people from days long gone and take part in their daily activities’ (text of 2001 leafet).

Lost treasures of Iraq: war
BOX 7.5
and cultural heritage
The chaos that followed the 1991 Gulf
War and the subsequent Iraq War of
2003 had a devastating effect on Iraq’s
cultural heritage (Russell 1998; Brodie
2008; Stone and Bajjaly 2008). While
the direct consequences of war may be
unavoidable, the problems were made
worse by Western collectors and the
antiquities trade as well as by military
activity. Cultural heritage is – in theory
– protected during confict by the 1954
Hague Convention (Cole 2008: 65), but
this has often been ignored. In some
(Image source: 615 collection/Alamy Stock Photo)
instances cultural heritage has been
deliberately targeted in warfare, as in the
former Yugoslavia in the 1990s where historic buildings (especially churches and mosques) were
bound up with rival national, religious or ethnic identities, and in the iconoclasm undertaken by the
Islamic State in Syria and Iraq (Barker 2018). In Iraq, looting of the national museum in Baghdad led
to the loss of thousands of archaeological objects, some of them extremely rare. Many ended up in
the hands of antiquities collectors around the world, although a proportion were found and returned
to the museum. Elsewhere military camps situated on ancient cities, including Ur (pictured here) and
Babel, led to damage of the archaeological remains by the digging of defensive trenches (Moussa
2008). Archaeologists face ethical dilemmas when trying to protect archaeological sites and artefacts
in the midst of war, when generals and politicians will have quite different priorities (Stone and Bajjaly
2008; Stone 2011, 2013; Hamilakis 2009).
Archaeology and ethics: the
BOX 7.6
case of human remains
Engagement with the public, media archaeology, the trade in antiquities, the nature of museum
displays and how we manage heritage all raise ethical questions for archaeologists. Ethics are
particularly signifcant when dealing with human remains (Scarre and Scarre 2006; Zimmerman et
al. 2003; Cassman et al. 2007; Roberts 2018: 17–38; Sayer 2017b). Diverse groups of people in
many countries have requested the return and reburial of human remains on the basis of beliefs and
ancestral connections of the kind given legal recognition by the Native American Graves Protection
and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) in the USA (p. 319). In the USA, Australia and New Zealand, these
concerns have long been recognised, but only recently has reburial been more widely demanded in
Britain. Whereas many medieval and postmedieval bodies have been reburied because of specifc
Christian or Jewish associations, few earlier remains have such direct connections (Roberts and Cox
2003). Since the 2000s, however, modern British pagans have argued that they have rights over
archaeological material from prehistoric Britain (Wallis and Blain 2011; Sayer 2017b; Honouring the
Ancient Dead 2023). This has led to demands that excavated human bones and their associated grave

THE PAST IN THE PRESENT AND THE FUTURE 373
goods from multiple contexts, such as Neolithic remains dating from c. 3700–2000 BC in Avebury
Museum, Wiltshire, should be reburied, and that other remains, such as the Iron Age bog-body
known as Lindow Man found in Cheshire, should be ‘repatriated’ to their places of discovery. Ethical
codes of practice have been drawn up in order to guide archaeologists in these circumstances.
The Vermillion Accord was adopted by the World Archaeological Congress in 1989, and the British
Association for Biological Anthropology and Osteoarchaeology has drawn up a similar guide (Babao
2019). The Vermillion Accord states that, when dealing with human remains:
• R espect for the mortal remains of the dead shall be accorded to all, irrespective of origin,
race, religion, nationality, custom and tradition.
• R espect for the wishes of the dead concerning disposition shall be accorded whenever
possible, reasonable and lawful, when they are known or can be reasonably inferred.
• R espect for the wishes of the local community and of relatives or guardians of the dead shall
be accorded whenever possible, reasonable and lawful.
• R espect for the scientifc research value of skeletal, mummifed and other human remains
(including fossil hominids) shall be accorded when such value is demonstrated to exist.
• A greement on the disposition of fossil, skeletal, mummifed and other remains shall be reached
by negotiation on the basis of mutual respect for the legitimate concerns of communities for the
proper disposition of their ancestors, as well as the legitimate concerns of science and education.
• T he express recognition that the concerns of various ethnic groups, as well as those of
science are legitimate and to be respected, will permit acceptable agreements to be reached
and honoured (https://worldarch.org/code-of-ethics/).
These criteria are easier to apply in places where direct ancestor communities exist, but in places
like Britain there has been considerable debate as to who the modern guardians of the ancient dead
are. Even with advances in aDNA studies, it is unlikely that there is any direct biological relationship
between those buried at Avebury and people living in Britain today, and modern pagan practices
and beliefs have little, if anything, in common with those of the Iron Age, when Lindow Man was
ritually killed. Do the claims of those who hold pagan beliefs have the same validity as those of
archaeologists and broader public opinion? Advances in archaeological techniques for analysing human
remains (Chapter 5) are providing an astonishing amount of new knowledge about past peoples –
their origins, diets and social organisation, as well as about the origins and development of human
diseases. Does this strengthen the argument for the view that human remains should be retained to
allow for future research which will inform all of us (including modern pagans) about past societies
and belief systems? Ethical guidelines undoubtedly help, but questions about the ‘ownership’ of
human remains require wide and well-informed public debate and a dialogue between stakeholders
to address confict and ensure participatory decision making (Wallis and Blain 2011; Sayer 2017b).

Heritage Futures: The future of nuclear waste
BOX 7.7
Nuclear waste may not seem, at frst glance, like it has anything to do with archaeology or heritage.
However, it is something that archaeologists and heritage practitioners have given a great deal of
consideration in the last decade. This is because the waste from the generation of nuclear power is so
highly radioactive that it takes a minimum of a hundred thousand years to be deemed safe. This means
that anyone who is producing it must also fnd a safe way to dispose of it which ensures not only the
safety of living populations, but also of future generations. The primary method of disposal for this waste
is to place it in drilled tunnels in geologically stable rock deep below the Earth’s surface. The tunnels will
then be flled with concrete and sealed. However, a central concern for nuclear waste management
companies is the question of how they can communicate the danger of these sites to future generations.
This is where archaeologists and heritage practitioners have played a role, because marking this danger
is not merely a question of leaving a simple sign or carving. In the hundred thousand years it takes for
nuclear waste to be deemed safe, ice ages may scour the Earth, languages may change and
we cannot even be sure that the hominids or other sentient biological organisms receiving
our messages will belong to the species Homo sapiens, which is not older than c.300,000
years and may not exist in the same form a few hundred thousand years ahead. No one

380 THE PAST IN THE PRESENT AND THE FUTURE
can honestly claim to be able to transmit information reliably many thousands of years into
the future.
(Wollentz et al. 2020: 296)
In some cases, such as at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico, United States, the use
of monuments and sculptures which draw upon shapes from nature which indicate danger have been
considered as one way of communicating with future populations (Joyce 2020). Elsewhere Dawney
et al. (2017) have drawn upon the posthuman theoretical perspectives outlined in Chapter 6 to think
about the ‘ONKALO Project’, a vast nuclear waste repository in Finland. Here they suggest that we
can address the questions of communication through time by using mixtures of sounds, spaces and
material culture to create ‘materially affective atmospheres’, places that ‘feel’ uncomfortable, which
may act to deter future users from the site. Through this approach, they argue,
We can attempt to think across millennia, to think about our worlds and future worlds as
entanglements of technologies and bodies, of affects and atmospheres within which we can
attempt to gain points of purchase through that which may be shared, or held in common.
(Dawney et al. 2017: 123–24)
In Sweden Holtorf and Högberg (2014, 2016, 2021) have considered this problem in collaboration
with SKB, the Swedish Nuclear Waste Management Company, at the long-term nuclear waste and
spent fuel repository site in Forsmark (pictured below). Here they have taken a different approach,
asking, ‘What happens when we come to see nuclear waste as heritage?’ (Harrison et al. 2020: 11).
That is, what if we recognise that the site will always have different heritage values and be interpreted
differently over time? In this case, they conclude, that ‘the best chance to transmit knowledge and
information in the long-term is thus to keep knowledge alive in the short and medium terms, inviting
future generations to interpret and use
these sites in their own way’ (Holtorf
and Högberg 2020: 651).
However such sites ultimately
choose to communicate their danger
to future peoples, Joyce’s (2020)
work examining several nuclear
waste facilities in the United States
shows that even in the present these
solutions are deeply complex. Joyce’s
study highlights the ethical, political
and temporal issues, not just around
the storage of radioactive waste itself,
but also the use of ancestral lands of

382 THE PAST IN THE PRESENT AND THE FUTURE
A passport to the past: archaeological skills
BOX 7.8
passports and continuous professional development
Whatever country you are based in, the chances are
you may have used a version of an archaeological
skills passport for recording and refecting upon
your development of archaeological and transferrable
skills. The frst skills passports were developed in
the UK in the 2000s by David Connolly from British
Archaeological Jobs and Resources (BAJR), Hannah
Cobb (University of Manchester) and Phil Richardson
(Archaeology Scotland) on the ‘Ardnamurchan
Transitions Project’. In 2010, supported by a grant from
the UK’s Higher Education Academy, Cobb, Connolly
and Richardson (together with other colleagues from
the University of Manchester) created the frst hard-
copy passport document (pictured). Subsequently,
this free-to-access document has been adopted and
adapted in higher education institutions around the
world, while BAJR has produced an updated and
more comprehensive commercially available version.
There are now Welsh and German language versions
of the passport, with Arabic and Italian versions in
preparation, as well as an Australian version which
incorporates the important perspective of Indigenous (Image source: Hannah Cobb)
knowledge-holders. The themes of the passport have also shaped archaeology modules available
universally online, such as DigVentures ‘virtual feld school’, whilst some commercial archaeological
organisations have developed their own versions.
Whether or not you have used a skills passport, the underlying principles of the document can
be used by anyone. Its primary aims are to document skills development (which then helps with
activities like CV writing), and to encourage people in the early stages of their archaeological education
and career to actively refect upon the skills they have gained, and to consider how to develop
them further. This practice of refection and development is known as continuous professional
development (CPD) and, whether students end up working in archaeology, elsewhere in the CRM
or heritage sector or in a different type of employment entirely, CPD is an excellent habit to get
into. Doing CPD can be as simple as attending a conference, workshop or webinar, but it can also
involve receiving specifc training in new skills or refreshing one’s existing knowledge. CPD ensures
that practitioners keep up to date with the latest developments in their area of work, and it also
ensures that they are practising to the highest standards. Consequently, CPD is highly valued by
many employers and professional organisations. The UK’s professional archaeological organisation,
the Chartered Institute for Archaeologists, asks members to undertake ffty hours of CPD every two
years in order to maintain the highest professional standards.
